messages.subject: Re: zigzag sampler error
parts:
Dear Paul, List,

This is not the full answer to your question, others might have further=20
suggestions.

There is a potential issue with your approach. Remember distance=20
sampling requires that transects are placed randomly with respect to=20
animal distribution. This is so because conventional methods assume that=20
the distribution of animals, detected or not, is known (uniform in the=20
case of line transects, triangular in the case of points), and given the=20
random placement of a sufficient number of transects, that known=20
distribution is obtained (on average). Because it is not likely that=20
animals are uniformly distributed in altitude, the detection function=20
from a point in the ground is inevitably confounded with that altitude=20
density gradient, and hence you might hit problems if you try to use=20
distance sampling in that context.

A possible approach could be to have independent observers, which would=20
then allow you not to depend on a known animal distribution in altitude.=20
A related example is described in the Advanced Distance Sampling book,=20
section 11.8, in which migration counts of whales are carried from a=20
point on the shore. Another alternative would be to try to incorporate=20
the information on the altitude gradient in the process, but this is not=20
necessarily straightforward.

Cheers,

Tiago

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: zigzag sampler error
parts:
Paul, in this set-up, you can't assume that the birds are uniformly
distributed with respect to perpendicular distance from the observation
point. You may want to look at the section on migration counts (section
11.8 of Advanced Distance Sampling - also see the 1993 distance sampling
book) and see whether you can apply that approach. With double
observers, it could work very well.

Steve Buckland
